name: Canaima National Park
blurb: Tepui plateaus, pitcher plants and the jaguar of the Gran Sabana.

tip.title: Thin out the ants
tip.text: Ants feed pitcher plants, frogs, anteaters and armadillos. Set Ants to -100% and follow the ripple up to the jaguar.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Canaima National Park, Gran Sabana, Heliamphora). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Savanna grasses and sedges
nodes.desc: Grasses and sedges cover the open Gran Sabana, growing on rocky, sandy, nutrient-poor soils derived from sandstone.

nodes.name: Miconia
nodes.desc: Berry-bearing shrubs and small trees among the most recorded plants around the park; GloBI records show bananaquits and tanagers eating their fruit.

nodes.name: Ants
nodes.desc: Abundant forest and savanna insects. They are the main prey caught by Heliamphora pitchers and a staple for anteaters, armadillos and frogs.
A large browser and fruit-eater named among the Gran Sabana's mammals; a big prey animal for jaguars.
Eats mostly ants and termites, dug from nests with its claws. Only jaguars and pumas are known to hunt adults.
One of the most recorded birds near the park; it feeds on carrion, helping return dead animals to the ecosystem.
A huge forest eagle that hunts mostly tree-dwelling mammals, sloths above all, and sometimes young deer.
The top predator of the park. It hunts large mammals such as tapirs and deer, and is one of the few animals known to hunt adult giant anteaters.
Powers the grasslands and forest; tepui summits are often wrapped in cloud.

nodes.name: Fungi, bacteria & litter fauna
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the thin soil.

story: Canaima National Park covers 30,000 km² of southeastern Venezuela, roughly the size of Belgium. About 65% is tepuis, flat-topped sandstone mountains with vertical walls. Auyantepui is the site of Angel Falls, the world's highest waterfall at 979 metres.
matters: The Pemon people live here and have an intimate relationship with the tepuis. A 2017 IUCN assessment listed the park as an area of significant concern, citing ineffective protection and management.
